headline: New-moon springs load the rips as bass push the boulder field and fluke slide to the reefs
subhead: Bigger water and a PM flood lining up with sunset have the Point fishing on a schedule again — here's where to be and when.
body_markdown:
Last week the Point was still living off the tail end of the June full moon — decent push through the rips but nothing that made you plan your whole day around it. That's changing fast. We're sliding into new-moon springs now, peak alignment falling right in this Friday-through-Monday window, and the difference in current speed at North Bar and Shagwong Reef is already noticeable on the drift. Bigger tidal range means more water moving through the boulder field on both stages, which means bait gets pinned harder against structure and bass don't have to work as hard to eat. The other piece that matters this week: the PM flood is starting to converge with sunset again, the first time that's lined up since the full moon in June. That's the window I circle on the calendar every summer — low light, moving water, and bass willing to come up.

Water's been stable and on the warmer side of comfortable, nothing extreme, but it's enough to keep bait staged tight to structure rather than spread out over open sand. Wind's been the bigger factor — we had a stretch of it out of the southwest that chopped up the surface off the Lighthouse and made the boulder field sloppy to fish on foot. If that lays down even a little this week, and the forecast suggests it should ease into more manageable conditions by midweek, the Point becomes fishable again on the stages that actually matter — the last two hours of the incoming into the top, and the first hour of the outgoing when everything starts draining hard through the rip.

Bass fishing has been real but it's not a gimme. I've had nights at the boulder field where three drifts through the rip on the incoming produced fish in the 20s and 30s, mixed with a couple that felt heavier than that in the dark — one push of bigger fish came through on eels fished dead slow, just enough action to keep the tail working, right where the white water meets the sand shelf drop. Bucktails in white and chartreuse, 1.5 to 2 ounces depending on how hard the current's running, have been the daytime play at Shagwong Reef, worked with a slow lift-and-drop through the boulder tops in 15 to 25 feet. Topwater's been a mixed bag — some mornings the pencil poppers get walked through busting fish at first light off Turtle Cove, other mornings it's dead calm and you're better off switching to a paddle-tail swim shad worked deeper. That inconsistency is the honest read right now: the fish are there, but you need to be on the right stage of tide to get them to commit on top. Fly guys working sand eel patterns and small Deceivers on sinking heads have done well drifting the same rips at first light, particularly when the outgoing starts pulling bait off the bar.

Bluefish have been mixed into the same water, which is normal for July — chopper blues cutting through bass schools at the rip edges, happy to jump on diamond jigs or the same poppers meant for stripers. If you're marking bait stacked tight on the sounder off North Bar and getting torn-up leaders, that's your answer as to who's under there.

Fluke have shifted hard toward the ocean side and the inlet-adjacent structure, which tracks with what's happening in the bays right now — Gardiners Bay and the harbor have gotten warm enough that the fluke are sliding out to cooler, cleaner water pushing up from offshore. I've been finding better numbers drifting the reef structure off the harbor entrance and along the deeper edges toward Frisbee's, working 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, staying tight to the bottom on the outgoing when the current's got enough push to keep the bait moving without you having to add weight. Not a banner week — for every keeper you're picking through a handful of shorts — but the quality fish, a few pushing 5 and 6 pounds, have been coming from the deeper pockets where that upwelled ocean water is holding, not the shallow flats that were producing back in June.

Weakfish remain a ghost around here — I haven't heard a credible report in weeks despite water temps that should theoretically support them. That fishery's been a disappointment up and down the coast this summer and Montauk's no exception. Porgies are around the reef structure in decent numbers if you want an easy box of fish on standard high-low rigs with clam, but nobody's writing home about it.

Looking ahead: if the wind cooperates and lays down through midweek, I'd be at the boulder field for the Friday and Saturday evening flood, right as it lines up with sunset — that's the best structural setup we've had since the last full moon, and the bigger tidal push should stack bait harder against the reef. Guys working the eastern inlets have already started seeing the first signs of bonito and false albacore pushing in on clean incoming water, which tells me the fall pelagic pattern is starting to stage early this year — worth keeping half an eye out around the rips once the bass activity slows midday. My plan is simple: work the dawn and dusk tides at the Point for bass, hit the reef structure for fluke on the ocean-side drift when the sun's high, and stay flexible if that albie window opens up faster than expected.
